data.name: Introduction
data.text:
Retatrutide, a novel synthetic molecule, which shows potent agonist action at the GIPR, GLP- 1R, and GCGR is being developed for improving glycemic control and for chronic weight management. It has a chemical structure and pharmacologic profile that is distinct from the GLP- 1 RAs and from GIP/GLP-1 RAs due to the additional effects on GCGRs, which is unique among the approved incretin mimetics. It is administered QW by SC injection. Preclinical and Phase 1 and 2 clinical data have shown improved glycemic control, weight reduction, and improvement in other key cardiometabolic parameters relevant for patients with T2D (Coskun et

al. 2022; Urva et al. 2022; Rosenstock et al. 2023).

The 2 estimands, treatment regimen estimand and efficacy estimand, address ICEs using the treatment policy strategy and the hypothetical strategy, respectively. The treatment regimen estimand will be the primary estimand, with the efficacy estimand considered supportive.

Treatment policy strategy The occurrence of the ICE is considered irrelevant in defining the treatment effect of interest; the values for the variable of interest are used regardless of whether the ICE occurs.

Hypothetical strategy A scenario is envisaged in which the ICE would not occur. The value of the variable to reflect the clinical question of interest is the value that the variable would have taken in the hypothetical scenario defined.

Treatment regimen estimand The clinical question of interest is: What is the treatment difference in the change in HbA1c from baseline at Week 40 between retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, and/or 12 mg compared with placebo in individuals who meet the eligibility criteria regardless of adherence to study intervention or initiation of additional antihyperglycemic medications? Treatment regimen estimand attributes

• Population - the target population is the group of individuals who meet the eligibility criteria. For the analysis, the intent-to-treatment principle will be applied.

• Endpoint - change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 40.

• Treatment condition - the randomly assigned treatment with allowance for potential dose interruptions and dose modification regardless of adherence to study intervention or initiation of additional antihyperglycemic medications.

• Intercurrent events - no ICEs are defined since treatment adherence and the initiation of additional antihyperglycemic medications are a part of the treatment condition.

Rationale for the efficacy estimand This estimand aims to evaluate the efficacy of retatrutide under the ideal condition that all participants would adhere to the randomly assigned study intervention without being confounded by the initiation of additional antihyperglycemic medications.

Efficacy estimand attributes

• Population - the target population is the group of individuals who meet the eligibility criteria. For the analysis, the intent-to-treatment principle will be applied.

• Endpoint - change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 40.

• Treatment condition - the randomly assigned treatment with allowance for potential dose interruptions and dose modifications.

• Intercurrent events - ICEs include permanent discontinuation of study intervention and initiation of additional antihyperglycemic medications and will be handled by the hypothetical strategy. Study procedures and their timing are summarized in the SoA.

Section 10.2 lists the laboratory tests that will be performed for this study.

Immediate safety concerns should be discussed with the sponsor immediately upon occurrence or awareness to determine if the participant should continue or discontinue study intervention.

Adherence to the study design requirements, including those specified in the SoA, is essential and required for study conduct.

All screening evaluations must be completed and reviewed to confirm that potential participants meet all eligibility criteria. The investigator will maintain a screening log to record details of all participants screened and to confirm eligibility or record reasons for screening failure, as applicable.

Overall Design:

Study GZBY is a Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, parallel-arm, double-blind, placebo- controlled study to investigate the efficacy and safety of retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg compared with placebo in participants with T2D and inadequate glycemic control with diet and exercise alone, are naïve to insulin use and have not been treated with any antihyperglycemic medication during the 90 days preceding Visit 1.

Brief Summary:

The purpose of this study is to investigate the efficacy and safety of retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg administered QW for 40 weeks compared with placebo for mean change from baseline in HbA1c in participants with T2D and inadequate glycemic control with diet and exercise alone.

data.name: Study Rationale
data.text: Study GZBY is designed to determine the comparative benefits and risks of retatrutide versus placebo, in participants with T2D who have inadequate glycemic control with diet and exercise alone, are naive of insulin therapy except for gestational diabetes or ≤14 days use for acute treatment and have not been treated with any oral glucose-lowering medication or noninsulin injectables within 90 days prior to study entry. Additionally, the study will compare the effects of retatrutide and placebo on body weight and overall safety profile.

data.name: Background
data.text:
Type 2 diabetes T2D is a metabolic condition characterized by impaired glycemic control caused by increased insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell failure and consequently inadequate insulin secretion (Zheng et al. 2018). T2D is frequently associated with comorbidities such as overweight or obesity, hypertension, increased blood lipoprotein concentrations, and a higher risk for macro- and microvascular complications. Achieving an HbA1c target of <7% has been shown to reduce microvascular complications of T2D when instituted early in the course of disease and more stringent goals may be appropriate and beneficial for certain individuals (ADA 2023). Following a person-centered holistic approach, ADA standards of care in diabetes (ADA 2023) also outline the importance of selection of a treatment regimen that supports weight management goals.

Unmet needs for diabetes treatment With the prevalence of T2D increasing worldwide, new antihyperglycemic agents offering significant improvements in glycemic control and additional weight loss as well as other potential health benefits, which would result in improved health outcomes, are highly desired.

Injectable incretin-based treatments are commonly used in combination with oral antihyperglycemic medication to achieve and maintain glucose control (ADA 2023). These treatment options offer improved glycemic control, low risk of hypoglycemia, and the potential for clinically relevant weight reduction. However, a proportion of patients do not reach individualized treatment targets despite high levels of compliance with the treatment regimens.

Therefore, there is an unmet need for additional treatment options that enhance glycemic control, promote weight reduction, and preserve an acceptable benefit/risk profile.

39 Clinical data for retatrutide A detailed description of the chemistry, pharmacology, efficacy, and safety of retatrutide is provided in the IB. Currently, two Phase 2 studies of retatrutide have been completed.

Phase 2 study in patients with T2D Study J1I-MC-GZBD was a 36-week, Phase 2, multicenter, randomized, double-blind study of QW retatrutide compared with placebo and dulaglutide (1.5 mg) in participants with T2D. Four maintenance doses of retatrutide were evaluated in the study, 0.5 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg, and 12 mg with the primary outcome of change from baseline in HbA1c (Rosenstock et al. 2023).

Key efficacy and safety data at 36 weeks

• HbA1c change from baseline was -0.3% for placebo, -1.4% for dulaglutide 1.5 mg, and - 1.3% to -2.2% for retatrutide (4 mg to 12 mg).

• HbA1c targets of <7% and ≤6.5% were achieved by 60% and 43% of participants treated with dulaglutide 1.5 mg, respectively, and 59% to 82% and 45% to 82% of participants treated with retatrutide (4 mg to 12 mg), respectively.

• Body weight change from baseline was -3% for placebo, -2% for dulaglutide 1.5 mg and -7.9% to -16.9% for retatrutide (4 mg to 12 mg).

• Body weight reduction of at least 5%, 10%, and 20% were achieved by 17%, 2%, and 0% of participants treated with dulaglutide 1.5 mg, respectively, and 61% to 94%, 22% to 75%, and 9% to 40% of participants treated with retatrutide (4 mg to 12 mg), respectively.

• The overall safety profile of retatrutide was consistent with that of the GLP-1 RA class in people with T2D, with most common TEAEs being GI related (including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation). The majority of GI AEs were mild to moderate in severity and occurred mostly during the dose escalation period and decreased over time.

Data from Phase 2 studies demonstrated the efficacy and safety of multiple retatrutide doses administered QW and support continued development of retatrutide for T2D.

data.name: Benefit/Risk Assessment
data.text:
Detailed information about the known and expected benefits and risks and reasonably expected AEs of retatrutide may be found in the IB.

2.3.1.

Risk Assessment Risks associated with retatrutide The identified risks and potential risks associated with retatrutide are similar to those of marketed GLP-1 RAs and the GIP/GLP-1 RA, tirzepatide.

The most commonly reported TEAEs observed in the retatrutide clinical studies, in healthy participants or participants with T2D, are GI effects, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Other risks and potential risks associated with retatrutide include

• Acute pancreatitis 40

• Increases in HR and decreases in systolic BP

• Hypoglycemia when used with sulfonylureas or insulin

• Thyroid C-cell tumors (only observed in rodents with long-acting GLP-1 RAs and GIP/GLP-1 RA), and

• Skin burning sensation and related AEs.

Sections 5.1, 5.2, and 8.2 address mitigation, management, and monitoring of the known risks and potential risks associated with retatrutide.

Study procedures Blood draws Risks of blood draws for clinical laboratory assessments include the potential for some pain and a small risk of bruising or infection at the site.

ECG collection Collection of ECGs may cause mild discomfort during placement and removal of leads from the skin. Some participants may experience local irritation or redness at the sites of lead attachment.

Retinal assessment Dilating drops, if used for pupil dilation for the eye examination, may sting temporarily and may cause temporary blurred vision, difficulty focusing, and light sensitivity. Pharmacologic dilatation may be contraindicated in some participants with eye conditions, for example, closed angle glaucoma.

2.3.2.

Benefit Assessment Data from Phase 2 studies of retatrutide supports an expectation of improved glycemic control and weight reduction in patients with T2D. Improvements in some cardiometabolic risk factors, including BP and serum lipids, may also be expected in this patient population.

Participants may also benefit from receiving personal health information, diabetes education, routine safety assessments, and frequent engagement with healthcare providers during the study, which provide opportunities for coaching and support.

2.3.3. Overall Benefit Risk Conclusion The safety and efficacy profile seen to date for retatrutide supports the overall benefit risk for participants in this study. Considering the measures taken to minimize risk to participants in this study, the potential risks identified in association with retatrutide are outweighed by the anticipated benefits that may be afforded to participants living with diabetes.

41

data.name: Overall Design
data.text:
Study GZBY is a Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, parallel-arm, double-blind, placebo- controlled study to investigate the efficacy and safety of retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg compared with placebo in participants with T2D and inadequate glycemic control with diet and exercise alone, are naïve to insulin use and have not been treated with any antihyperglycemic medication during the 90 days preceding Visit 1.

Approximately 480 participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to retatrutide 4 mg (approximately 120), retatrutide 9 mg (approximately 120), retatrutide 12 mg (approximately 120), and placebo (approximately 120), respectively.

This study will consist of 3 periods:

• a screening period: up to 4 weeks

• a treatment period: 40 weeks, including dose escalation and maintenance, and

• a safety follow-up period: 4 weeks.

data.name: Scientific Rationale for Study Design
data.text:
Choice of primary endpoint The primary endpoint of HbA1c is a commonly used endpoint in clinical trials evaluating the efficacy and safety of antihyperglycemic agents.

Choice of comparator Regulatory authorities require the safety profile of new drugs to be well-characterized, including a sufficient number of placebo exposures. Per ICH E 1 (EMEA 1995), a placebo-controlled design is necessary to directly compare the AE rate in the drug-treated group with the background event rate in the patient population being studied.

Double-blind design A double-blind design was selected to minimize participant and investigator bias in assessments for efficacy, safety, and study intervention tolerability.

Duration of the study treatment The planned duration of the study treatment for 40 weeks is considered sufficient and appropriate for participants to optimize dosing of retatrutide and to assess the full effects and benefit/risk of each treatment dose of retatrutide on glycemic control.

Collection of race and ethnicity data In this study, collection of demographic information includes race and ethnicity. The scientific rationale is based on the need to assess variable response in safety and/or efficacy based on race or ethnicity. This question can be answered only if all the relevant data are collected.

46

data.name: Justification for Dose
data.text:
Retatrutide doses of 4 mg, 9 mg, and 12 mg QW will be evaluated in this study for assessment of efficacy and safety for glycemic control in patients with T2D.

These doses and associated escalation scheme were selected based on assessment of safety, efficacy, (improvement in glycemic control and body weight reduction), tolerability data, and PK/PD exposure–response modeling of data from Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies.

Participants randomly assigned to retatrutide will start with a 2 mg QW dose and have a dose escalation every 4 weeks until the 4 mg, 9 mg or 12 mg dose is reached. This dose escalation scheme is designed to minimize GI tolerability concerns.

The maintenance doses of 4 mg, 9 mg, and 12 mg are expected to provide clinically relevant glycemic control relative to placebo with increasing efficacy with increasing dose.

The selected dose levels and dose range will support a robust dose–exposure–response analysis of multiple safety and efficacy measures to support further evaluation of the benefit/risk of the selected retatrutide doses.

data.name: Inclusion Criteria
data.text:
Participants are eligible to be included in the study only if all of the following criteria apply:

Age

1. Participant must be at least 18 years of age or the legal age of consent in the jurisdiction in which the study is taking place at the time of signing the informed consent, whichever is older.

Type of participant and disease characteristics

2. Have a clinical diagnosis of T2D based on the World Health Organization classification or other locally applicable diagnostic standards (see Section 10.8).

3. Have HbA1c ≥7.0% (53 mmol/mol) to ≤9.5% (80 mmol/mol) despite diet and exercise treatment, as determined by the central laboratory at Visit 1 (screening).

4. Are naïve to insulin therapy except for gestational diabetes or ≤14 days use for acute treatment and have not used any oral or injectable antihyperglycemic medications during the 90 days preceding Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3 (randomization).

5. Are motivated and willing to make themselves available for the duration of the study and are able to follow study procedures as required, including

• store provided study intervention as directed

• perform SMBG per protocol

• maintain a study eDiary

• complete patient questionnaires, and

• self-inject study intervention.

Note: Persons with physical limitations who are not able to perform the injections must have the assistance of an individual trained to inject the intervention.

Weight

6. Are of stable weight (self-reported change ≤5 kg or 11 pounds) for at least 90 days prior to Visit 1 and agree to not initiate an intensive diet or exercise program during the study with the intent of reducing body weight other than the lifestyle and/or dietary measures for diabetes treatment.

7. Have a BMI ≥23.0 kg/m2 at Visit 1.

48 Sex and contraceptive/barrier requirements

8. Males, WOCBP, or WNOCBP may participate in this trial.

Contraceptive use by participants should be consistent with local regulations regarding the methods of contraception for those participating in clinical studies. For the contraception requirements of this protocol, see Section 10.4.

Note: the word “male” is used to describe an individual assigned male at birth (AMAB) and the word “female” is used to describe an individual assigned female at birth (AFAB), for simplicity.

Informed consent

9. Are capable of giving signed informed consent as described in Section 10.1.3, which includes compliance with the requirements and restrictions listed in the ICF and in this protocol.

data.name: Exclusion Criteria
data.text:
Participants are excluded from the study if any of the following criteria apply:

Medical conditions Diabetes-related

10. Have T1D.

11. Have a history of ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state or coma within the last 6 months prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3.

12. Have a history of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness within the last 6 months prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3.

13. Are currently receiving or planning to receive treatment for diabetic retinopathy and/or macular edema, for example, laser photocoagulation or intravitreal injections of anti- vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors.

Note: All participants will have a baseline fundus photography assessment. In the presence of any degree of diabetic retinopathy and/or macular edema, further ophthalmologic assessment will follow local standards of care to confirm eligibility.

Obesity-related

14. Have a prior or planned surgical treatment for obesity Exceptions: The following are allowed if they occurred >1 year before screening (Visit 1):

• liposuction

• cryolipolysis, or

• abdominoplasty.

49

15. Have a prior or planned endoscopic (for example, mucosal ablation or gastric artery embolization) and/or device-based (for example, lap band, intragastric balloon, or endoluminal duodenal-jejunal bypass liner) therapy for obesity.

Exception: Prior device-based therapy is acceptable if device removal was more than 6 months prior to screening (Visit 1).

Cardiovascular

16. Have New York Heart Association Functional Classification IV congestive heart failure.

17. Have had any of the following CV conditions within 90 days prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3:

• acute myocardial infarction

• cerebrovascular accident (stroke), or

• hospitalization for congestive heart failure.

Gastrointestinal

18. Have a known clinically significant gastric emptying abnormality, for example, severe diabetic gastroparesis or gastric outlet obstruction, or chronically take drugs that directly affect GI motility.

Hepatic

19. Have acute or chronic hepatitis, including a history of autoimmune hepatitis, signs or symptoms of any other liver disease other than MASLD, or any of the following as determined by the central laboratory during screening:

• ALT or AST level >5.0× ULN for the reference range

• ALP level ≥1.5× ULN for the reference range

• TBL level ≥1.5× ULN for the reference range, except for cases of known Gilbert’s syndrome

• hepatitis B infection, defined as o positive hepatitis B core antibody and positive for HBV DNA, or o positive hepatitis B surface antigen, and

• positive hepatitis C antibody and positive for HCV RNA.

Renal

20. Have an eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 as determined by the central laboratory at Visit 1 (calculated by Chronic Kidney Disease-Epidemiology cystatin-c equation).

Hematologic

21. Have any clinically relevant hematological condition that may interfere with HbA1c measurement, for example, hemolytic anemias or sickle cell disease.

50 Malignancy

22. Have a history of an active or untreated malignancy or are in remission from a malignancy for less than 5 years.

Exceptions: basal or squamous cell skin cancer, in situ carcinomas of the cervix, or in situ or Grade 1 (for example, Gleason 6 or lower) prostate cancer.

Endocrine

23. Have family (first-degree relative) or personal history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome Type 2.

24. Have a serum calcitonin level of

a. ≥20 pg/mL (≥5.9 pmol/L) at Visit 1, if eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and

b. ≥35 pg/mL (≥10.2 pmol/L) at Visit 1, if eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 as determined by the central laboratory at Visit 1.

Psychobehavioral

25. Have a history of unstable major depressive disorder or other severe psychiatric disorder, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or other serious mood or anxiety disorder, within the last 2 years.

OR In the investigator’s opinion, have any significant mental health disorder that may put the individual at higher risk of study participation.

26. Have a PHQ-9 score of 15 or more at Visit 1 or Visit 3.

27. Have any lifetime history of a suicide attempt.

28. Are, in the judgment of the investigator, actively suicidal and therefore deemed to be at significant risk for suicide.

29. Have answered “yes” to either Question 4 or Question 5 on the “Suicidal Ideation” portion of the C-SSRS, and the ideation occurred within the past month prior to Visit 1 or Visit 3.

OR Have answered “yes” to any of the suicide-related behaviors on the “Suicidal Behavior” portion of the C-SSRS, and the behavior occurred within the past month prior to Visit 1 or Visit 3.

General

30. Had chronic or acute pancreatitis any time.

31. Have had a transplanted organ or awaiting an organ transplant.

Exception: corneal transplants (keratoplasty).

Prior/concomitant therapy

32. Within 90 days prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3 51

• are receiving or have received chronic (>14 days) systemic glucocorticoid therapy, excluding topical, intraocular, intranasal, interphalangeal, or inhaled preparations, or

• have evidence of a significant, active autoimmune abnormality (for example, lupus or rheumatoid arthritis) that is likely to require, in the opinion of the investigator, such treatment during the study.

33. Have taken prescribed or over-the-counter medication, or alternative remedies, including herbal or nutritional supplements, intended to promote body weight reduction within 90 days prior to Visit 1, or between Visit 1 and Visit 3 (see Section 10.9 for examples).

34. Have started SC/intramuscular or implantable/injectable contraceptives such as Depo- Provera®, Nexplanon®, within 18 months prior to screening (Visit 1).

Note: Intrauterine devices are acceptable.

Prior/concurrent clinical trial experience

35. Are currently enrolled in any other clinical study involving an IP or any other type of medical research judged not to be scientifically or medically compatible with this study.

36. Have previously completed or withdrawn from this study or any other study investigating retatrutide after receiving at least 1 dose of study intervention (retatrutide, placebo, or an active comparator).

37. Have participated in a clinical study and received treatment, whether active or placebo within the last 30 days or duration equal to 5 times the half-life of study intervention, whichever is longer.

Other exclusion criteria

38. Have any condition, unwillingness, or inability not covered by any of the other exclusion criteria, that, in the opinion of the investigator, might

• jeopardize the safety of the participant; for example, allergies, intolerance, or hypersensitivity to GLP-1 RAs, GIP/GLP-1 RAs, or retatrutide or excipient or contraindication

• compromise compliance with the protocol; for example, recreational drug use or alcohol abuse, or

• confound data interpretation.

39. Are investigator site personnel directly affiliated with this study and/or their immediate families. Immediate family is defined as a spouse, parent, child, or sibling, whether biological or legally adopted.

40. Are Eli Lilly and Company employees or are employees of any third party involved in the study who requires exclusion of their employees.

41. Are pregnant or intend to become pregnant or to breastfeed during the study.

52

data.name: Lifestyle Considerations
data.text:
Throughout the study, participants will have access to qualified medical staff who will provide diabetes management counseling, which will include instructions on diet and exercise and education about the signs, symptoms, and treatment of hypoglycemia.

Participants should be counseled to continue their usual exercise habits and follow a healthy meal plan, with an emphasis on intake of healthy carbohydrate, protein, fat, and fluid.

Dietary counseling will be provided throughout the study, as needed. Per inclusion criterion 6 (Section 5.1), participants should not initiate during the study an organized diet or exercise weight reduction program other than the lifestyle and/or dietary measures for diabetes treatment.

For certain assessments, the participants will be required to come to the site in a fasting state, except for water, for at least 8 hours, as specified in the SoA.

5.3.1.

Diabetes Education Diabetes education is to be performed by personnel who are qualified to educate participants on symptoms and management of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia and diabetes management. All trainings should be repeated as needed to ensure participant compliance.

5.3.2.

Self-Monitoring of Blood Glucose (SMBG) At Visit 2, participants will receive a study-approved glucometer and related testing supplies for use during the study.

Site personnel will train the participant on correct use of the glucometer for SMBG and reporting of hypoglycemia. Participants will be instructed to monitor BG any time they have symptoms suggestive of hypoglycemia and will collect 4-point and 7-point SMBGs as outlined below.

Four-point SMBG Participants will be instructed to perform 4-point SMBG measurements once weekly during the treatment period and to record all results in the eDiary according to instructions; these results will be used for assessment of severe persistent hyperglycemia (Section 6.9.4). Four-point SMBG profiles will consist of measurements obtained on a single day

• before 3 main meals, and

• at bedtime.

During the weeks when the 7-point SMBG profiles are to be collected, participants will not be required to collect 4-point SMBG profiles, and the 4-point BG values included in the 7-point profiles may be used for assessment of severe persistent hyperglycemia.

Seven-point SMBG Participants will also be instructed to collect two 7-point SMBG profiles on non-consecutive days within 2 weeks prior to specified visits and record all results in the eDiary according to instructions preceding prespecified visits as shown in the SoA (Section 1.3); these results will be used for the efficacy analysis. Seven-point SMBG profiles will consist of measurements obtained on a single day

• before 3 main meals 53

• approximately 2 hours after 3 main meals, and

• at bedtime.

5.3.3.

Meals and Nutrition Participants will have access to qualified medical staff who will provide diabetes management counseling regarding a healthy diet.

Counseling considerations The focus of counseling should facilitate balanced and sufficient food and beverage choices for adequate nutritional intake and hydration. Counseling should include instruction on customized nutrient-dense food and beverage choices to reflect personal preferences, cultural traditions, and budgetary considerations.

Adequate nutritional intake and hydration recommendations may be individualized based on the participant’s health status, including age and comorbidities, appetite levels, and GI tolerability.

Recommendations should focus on prioritizing intake of healthy carbohydrate, protein, fat, and fluid.

Recommendations may include the following:

General daily intake recommendations Fluids (that is, water or decaffeinated and non- sugary beverages) >2000 to 3000 mL Energy a minimum of 800 to 1000 kcal (recommended energy intakes should be individualized based on factors like age, sex, and activity level).

Protein 0.8 to 1.5 g/kg, consider adjustment for participants with CKD (in some cases, calculation may be based on ideal body weight) Carbohydrates 45% to 65% of energy intake Fiber >21 g (women) >30 g (men) Fat 20% to 35% of energy intake Consider the following principles to guide participant education in counseling sessions:

• the importance of meeting nutritional and hydration recommendations

• decreased appetite and increased fullness after eating typically drive a reduction in food intake. Additional voluntary food restriction, when appetite is reduced, is unnecessary and may be harmful

• avoid skipping meals

• eat smaller, more frequent (every 3 to 4 hours) meals or snacks

• consider approximately ½ plate from fruits or vegetables, ¼ plate from whole grains, and ¼ plate from protein (from an 8-inch to 10-inch plate)

• include fiber-rich foods, and

• limit foods high in solid fats, added sugar, and salt.

54 In addition, the following strategies are encouraged to facilitate adequate nutritional intake and hydration:

• multivitamin and/or targeted micronutrient supplementation, as clinically appropriate

• meal replacements (for example, protein- and micronutrient-rich shakes or bars) that can be sipped or eaten slowly over several hours, particularly for participants with markedly reduced appetite and poor intake, and

• more frequent nutritional counseling, either in person or virtually, if needed (contact the Lilly Medical team with any questions for implementation).

5.3.4.

Monitoring Nutritional Needs Retatrutide has the potential for significant body weight reduction. It acts, in part, by reducing appetite leading to a reduction in food intake. There is a potential that some participants will have significantly reduced caloric intake.

Individual risk factors for poor nutrition or dehydration should be taken into consideration, including, but not limited to, age, medical history/comorbidities, concomitant medications, clinical conditions (for example, infection, renal function status), and GI symptoms (for example, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Clinically monitor the nutritional and hydration status of participants, and assess for any signs or symptoms of poor nutrition or dehydration, including

• vital signs

• targeted physical exam

• recent central laboratory data, and

• review of relevant adverse events and other signs or symptoms, such as fatigue, skin tenting, and dark-colored urine.

Obtain additional laboratory tests, as clinically appropriate, via the central laboratory. Use local laboratory tests as needed, for example, for acute management or if laboratory test is not available centrally. See Section 10.2 for more information on clinical laboratory tests.

By recognizing early signs of poor nutrition and dehydration, preventive actions can be taken to reduce the risk of potential complications.

Monitor for the following which could be risk factors/signs for poor nutrition or dehydration Potential concern Early signs include, but are not limited to Poor nutrition carbohydrate intake <50 g/day protein intake <60 g/day (minimum protein intake requirements may be different for participants with CKD) fat intake <15 g/day caloric intake <800 to 1000 kcal/day skipping multiple meals Dehydration low fluid intake (<2000 mL/day) volume loss (for example, diuretic or laxative use, diarrhea, vomiting) elevated pulse rate decreased or low BP high blood urea nitrogen to creatinine (BUN/Cr) ratio 55 If there are concerns for poor nutrition or dehydration, mitigations are based on an assessment of the severity of the participant’s status, potential underlying etiologies, and GI symptoms. See Sections 6.6.2 and 10.11 for the recommended steps to follow.

5.3.5.

Blood Donation Study participants should be instructed not to donate blood or blood products during the study, starting at Visit 1, and up to Visit 801 following the study.

data.text:
This table lists the interventions used in this clinical study.

Intervention Name Retatrutide Placebo Dosage Level(s) 2 mg 4 mga 6 mg 9 mga 12 mga Not applicable Route of Administration Subcutaneous injection QW Subcutaneous injection QW Abbreviation: QW = once weekly.

Packaging and labeling Study interventions will be supplied by the sponsor or its designee in accordance with current Good Manufacturing Practice. Study interventions will be labeled as appropriate for country requirements.

6.1.1.

Dose Escalation Schema Participants randomly assigned to retatrutide Participants randomly assigned to retatrutide, will start with a 2 mg QW dose and increase dose every 4 weeks until the randomly assigned maintenance dose (4 mg or 9 mg or 12 mg) is reached as outlined in the figure below.

To maintain blinding, participants randomly assigned to 4 mg and 9 mg will follow a sham dose escalation schedule to match the retatrutide 12 mg treatment group. For management of participants with intolerable GI symptoms, see Section 6.6.1.

Investigators, site staff, clinical monitors, and participants will remain blinded to the assigned maintenance dose of retatrutide, that is, 4 mg, 9 mg or 12 mg until the study is complete.

57 Participants randomly assigned to placebo To maintain blinding, participants randomly assigned to the placebo treatment group will also receive study intervention every 4 weeks during the dose escalation period, following a sham dose escalation schedule to match the retatrutide 12 mg group.

Timing of dose administration Participants should try to administer the SC injections on the same day of the week and similar time of day, but there are no restrictions on the time of day for each weekly dose.

The actual date and time of all dose administrations will be recorded by the participant in the participant diary. The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary, if the last dose was administered 72 or more hours before. If a dose is missed, the participant should take it as soon as possible unless it is within 72 hours of the next dose, in which case that dose should be skipped, and the next dose should be taken at the appropriate time. Participant should record the date and the reason the dose was not taken in the diary.

Anatomical location of injections Acceptable locations for injection by the participant include the abdomen or thigh, or upper arm if another person gives the injection.

Participants should rotate injection sites when injecting within the same region.

The participant will record the injection site location of all dose administrations in the diary.

6.1.2.

Medical Devices, Investigational Devices, or Device Constituents KwikPen device The Lilly manufactured medical device provided for use in this study is the multi-dose, single- patient use PFP. The PFP is a mechanical, prefilled, disposable pen injector system with a 3.0- mL cartridge for SC injection of retatrutide. The PFP is designed for once-weekly SC injection of study intervention for adult participants with T2D for doses listed in Section 6.1.

Instructions for device use and risks will be provided.

58 All PCs including malfunction shall be documented and reported by the investigator throughout the study (see Section 8.3) and appropriately managed by the sponsor.

data.name: Preparation, Handling, Storage, and Accountability
data.text:
The investigator or designee must confirm appropriate storage conditions have been maintained during transit for all study intervention received and any discrepancies are reported and resolved before use of the study intervention.

Only participants enrolled in the study may receive study intervention. Only authorized study personnel may supply, prepare, or administer study intervention.

All study intervention must be stored in a secure, environmentally controlled, and monitored (manual or automated) area in accordance with the labeled storage conditions with access limited to the investigator and authorized study personnel.

The investigator or authorized study personnel are responsible for study intervention accountability, reconciliation, and record maintenance, (that is, receipt, reconciliation, and final disposition records.

Further guidance and information for the final disposition of unused study interventions are provided in the Pharmacy Manual.

data.name: Assignment to Study Intervention
data.text:
Method of treatment assignment Participants who meet all criteria for enrollment will be randomly assigned to study intervention using an IWRS.

Study intervention will be dispensed at the study visits summarized in the SoA. Returned study intervention should not be re-dispensed to the participants.

Randomization ratios and stratification factors Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, 12 mg, or placebo.

Participants will be stratified based on

• country

• HbA1c (≤8.0%, >8.0%) at Visit 1, and

• prior use of any antihyperglycemic medication (yes or no).

data.name: Blinding
data.text:
This is a double-blind study. Investigators, site staff, clinical monitors, and participants will remain blinded to retatrutide or placebo until the final database lock.

To maintain the blind, a minimum number of Lilly personnel will see the randomization table and treatment assignments before the study is complete.

Unblinding details are specified in the blinding and unblinding plan.

59 Emergency unblinding In case of an emergency, the investigator has the sole responsibility for determining if unblinding of a participant’s treatment assignment is warranted for medical management of the event. The participant’s safety must always be the first consideration in making such a determination. If a participant’s treatment assignment is unblinded, Lilly must be notified immediately.

If the investigator decides that unblinding is warranted, it is the responsibility of the investigator to promptly document the decision and rationale and notify Lilly as soon as possible.

Emergency unblinding may be performed through the IWRS. This option may be used ONLY if the participant’s well-being requires knowledge of the participant’s treatment assignment. All unblinding events are recorded and reported by the IWRS.

Discontinuation from the study intervention in case of unblinding If an investigator, site personnel performing assessments, or participant is unblinded, the participant must be permanently discontinued from study intervention (Section 7.1.1) but should be continued in the study to be evaluated for efficacy and safety endpoints and monitored for all visits and testing.

data.name: Study Intervention Compliance
data.text:
Participant compliance with study intervention will be assessed as indicated in the SoA (Section 1.3). Compliance will be assessed by direct questioning and reviewing the eDiary and documented in the source documents and CRF.

Participants will be instructed to return any unused study intervention at the times specified in the SoA.

Treatment compliance for each visit interval is defined as taking at least 75% of the required doses of study intervention.

In addition to the assessment of a participant’s compliance with the study intervention administration, other aspects of compliance with the study will be assessed at each visit based on the participant’s adherence to the visit schedule, completion of study eDiaries, and any other parameters the investigator considers necessary.

Participants considered to be poorly compliant with their medication and/or the study procedures will receive additional training and instruction, as required, and will be reminded of the importance of complying with the protocol.

data.name: Dose Modification
data.text:
All dose adjustments for retatrutide and placebo will be managed through IWRS in a blinded fashion.

Dose modification is only allowed for the management of

• intolerable GI symptoms (Section 6.6.1)

• poor nutrition or dehydration (Sections 6.6.2 and 10.11)

• participant reaching a BMI ≤20 kg/m2 (Section 6.6.3), or 60

• perceived excessive weight reduction (Section 6.6.3).

6.6.1.

Management of Participants with GI Symptoms Dose modifications for intolerable GI symptoms can be initiated only during dose escalation (the first 20 weeks of the study).

Follow these steps if a participant reports intolerable GI symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea:

1. Counsel the participant on dietary behaviors that may help mitigate nausea and vomiting, for example,

a. eating smaller meals

b. splitting 3 daily meals into 4 or more smaller ones

c. stopping eating when they feel full, and

d. avoiding foods that trigger symptoms.

See Sections 5.3.3 and 5.3.4 for additional details.

2. If symptoms persist, prescribe symptomatic medication, for example, antiemetic, or antidiarrheal medication, per local country availability and individual participant needs.

Record these medications as concomitant medications in the CRF.

3. If Steps 1 and 2 do not alleviate intolerable GI symptoms, temporary interruption of study intervention for 1 dose is permitted, if the participant has taken the last 3 weekly injections (at any dose). Resume study intervention immediately, when possible, either alone or in combination with symptomatic medication.

4. If Steps 1, 2, and 3 do not alleviate intolerable GI symptoms during dose escalation, follow guidance for temporary dose de-escalation and dose re-escalation. Only 1 de-escalation and re-escalation attempt for intolerable GI symptoms will be permitted.

In the event of intolerable GI symptoms that occur after the dose escalation period, the investigator can advise on Steps 1 and 2 above (in other words, changes in dietary behaviors or consider prescribing symptomatic medication to keep the participant on study intervention) before stopping the treatment permanently.

6.6.1.1.

Temporary Dose De-escalation If intolerable GI symptoms persist despite the measures outlined in Steps 1 to 3 above (Section 6.6.1), during dose escalation, the investigator should contact the sponsor to consider de-escalating the dose to the next lower dose for 4 weeks in a blinded fashion. Dose de- escalation will occur as outlined in the following table.

61 If a participant is currently taking… Then dose will be de-escalated for 4 weeks to… 4 mg/Placebo 2 mg/Placebo 6 mg/Placebo 4 mg/Placebo 9 mg/Placebo 6 mg/Placebo 12 mg/Placebo 9 mg/Placebo Note: If intolerable GI symptoms occur and the participant is currently taking retatrutide 2 mg, then participant will discontinue the study intervention and continue in the study.

6.6.1.2.

Dose Re-escalation If intolerable GI symptoms persist with dose de-escalation described above, the participant should discontinue study intervention and continue in the study. If the participant is able to tolerate the de-escalated dose, the investigator must resume the dose escalation.

If the dose re-escalation results in the return of intolerable GI symptoms then the next step is dependent on whether or not the participant has reached the escalation or sham escalation to 6 mg dose.

If subsequent re-escalation is not tolerated and the participant is currently taking… Then dose will be de-escalated to… 6 mg/Placebo 4 mg or Placebo in a blinded fashion 9 mg/Placebo 6 mg or Placebo in a blinded fashion 12 mg/Placebo 9 mg or Placebo in a blinded fashion Note: If a participant does not tolerate retatrutide 4 mg, then the participant will discontinue the study intervention and continue in the study. No dose re-escalation is allowed. Participants in the 4-mg treatment group reaching a sham dose escalation to 6 mg or higher will switch to placebo to maintain the blind.

If intolerable GI symptoms persist despite dose de-escalation, the participant should discontinue study intervention. All participants who discontinue study intervention are encouraged to continue to attend the remaining scheduled study visits (see Section 7.1.1). The study participants who stop study intervention permanently, may receive another antihyperglycemic medication as allowed per protocol (see Section 6.9.4). The new glucose-lowering intervention will be recorded on the CRF specified for collecting antihyperglycemic medications.

6.6.2.

Management of Participants with Poor Nutrition or Dehydration Follow these steps (and refer to Section 10.11) if a participant is at risk of poor nutrition or dehydration based on clinical judgement and criteria described in Sections 5.3.3, 5.3.4, and 10.2.2:

1. Assess if there is an intercurrent illness (for example, systemic infection, cholecystitis,

etc) that could be causing or contributing to the inadequate oral intake.

a. If yes, consider a temporary interruption of study intervention per Section 6.6.4 until the illness has resolved.

b. If no, go to Step 2.

62

2. Assess if increased oral intake may likely trigger/worsen GI symptoms.

a. If no,

i. provide nutritional counseling and consider strategies to increase oral intake. Consider consultation with a registered dietitian (or local equivalent) if not already done. Refer to Sections 5.3.3 and 5.3.4.

ii. assess concomitant medications and consider adjustment as appropriate;

consider laboratory tests as appropriate (see Sections 10.10 and 10.2.2).

b. If yes,

i. temporarily interrupt the study intervention for 1 to 2 doses

ii. provide nutritional counseling and consider strategies to increase oral intake. Consider consultation with a registered dietitian (or local equivalent) if not already done. Refer to Sections 5.3.3 and 5.3.4

iii. assess concomitant medications and consider adjustment as appropriate;

consider laboratory tests as appropriate (see Sections 10.10 and 10.2.2).

iv. on reassessment, if nutritional and hydration concerns have resolved, restart study intervention per Section 6.6.4.

3. If nutritional and hydration concerns persist, contact the sponsor for possible dose reduction to the next lower dose or placebo in a blinded fashion. Dose reduction to retatrutide 2 mg is not allowed. If a participant is currently taking 4 mg retatrutide or 2 mg retatrutide, then the participant may discontinue the study intervention (retatrutide or placebo) permanently and continue in the study. No dose re-escalation is allowed.

4. Assess if the condition persists despite dose reduction.

a. If yes, discontinue the study intervention.

b. If no, continue the study intervention at the reduced dose.

Only 1 dose reduction for the management of participants with poor nutrition or dehydration, BMI ≤20 kg/m2, or perceived excessive weight reduction is allowed.

6.6.3.

Management of Participants with BMI ≤20 kg/m2 or Perceived Excessive Weight Reduction If … Then … a participant has a BMI ≤20 kg/m2 at any time during the study the investigator may contact the sponsor to consider a dose reduction to the next lower dose or placebo in a blinded fashion or discontinue the study intervention a participant has a BMI ≤18.5 kg/m2 at any time during the study the investigator must contact the sponsor to consider dose reduction to the next lower dose or placebo in a blinded fashion or discontinue the study intervention a participant with perceived excessive weight loss decides and wishes to discontinue from study intervention the investigator must contact the sponsor to consider dose reduction to the next lower dose or placebo in a blinded fashion or discontinue the study intervention 63 Note: Dose reduction to retatrutide 2 mg is not allowed. If a participant is currently taking 4 mg retatrutide or 2 mg retatrutide, then the participant may discontinue the study intervention (retatrutide or placebo) permanently and continue in the study. Participants in the 4-mg treatment group reaching a sham dose escalation to 6 mg or higher will switch to placebo to maintain the blind.

The decision of study intervention discontinuation or dose reduction will depend on several factors including timing of when these criteria are met, whether the participant is in weight reduction or weight maintenance phase, other comorbid conditions, concomitant medication, and AEs, and will be mutually agreed between sponsor and investigator to ensure safety of participants.

Only 1 dose reduction for the management of participants with poor nutrition or dehydration, BMI ≤20 kg/m2, or perceived excessive weight reduction is allowed. No dose re-escalation is allowed.

Participants with low BMI (≤20 kg/m2) should be assessed at least every 2 to 4 weeks for weight stabilization with either an in-office weight check or self-report via telehealth.

All participants who discontinue study intervention should be encouraged to continue to attend the remaining scheduled study visits and continue the study (see Section 7.1.1). Study participants who stop study intervention permanently should receive another antihyperglycemic medication as allowed per protocol (see Section 6.9.4). The new glucose-lowering intervention will be recorded on the CRF specified for collecting antihyperglycemic medications.

6.6.4.

Temporary Interruption of Study Intervention Unrelated to Gastrointestinal Tolerability In certain situations, the investigator may need to temporarily interrupt study intervention, for example, if the participant experiences acute illness, surgery, requires hospitalization, due to an AE unrelated to GI tolerability, or a clinically significant laboratory value. Every effort should be made by the investigator to maintain participants on study intervention and to restart study intervention after any temporary interruption, as soon as it is safe to do so.

When restarting study intervention, notify the sponsor at least 2 weeks prior to the dosing visit to ensure adequate study intervention supply at the site.

1. If the number of consecutive missed doses is ≤2, and the dose was well-tolerated prior to the interruption, then restart retatrutide at the same dose the participant received before the interruption or if during the first 20 weeks, the escalation will continue as planned.

2. If the number of consecutive missed doses is ≥3,

a. in the first 4 weeks of the study, restart retatrutide at 2 mg and subsequently escalate the dose as required by protocol.

b. after the first 4 weeks of the study, restart retatrutide at 4 mg, regardless of the dose the participant received before the interruption and subsequently escalate the dose as required by protocol.

3. The investigator will use the IWRS to receive the appropriate study intervention dispensing information to preserve blinding of the retatrutide dose.

64 The data related to temporary interruption of study intervention will be documented in source documents and entered on the CRF.

data.name: Treatment of Overdose
data.text:
For this study, any total dose of study intervention within a 72-hour period for retatrutide, greater than the dose assigned by IWRS for that participant will be considered a potential overdose and should be assessed for AE reporting as per criteria described in Section 10.3. In the event of an overdose, refer to the IB for retatrutide.

In the event of an overdose, the investigator should

• initiate supportive treatment according to the participant’s clinical signs and symptoms

• contact the medical monitor immediately

• evaluate the participant to determine, in consultation with the medical monitor, whether study intervention should be interrupted

• closely monitor the participant for any AE or SAE and laboratory abnormalities that could be associated with the overdose and initiate supportive treatment according to the participant’s clinical signs and symptoms, and

• obtain a plasma sample for PK analysis within 5 days from the date of the last dose of study intervention if requested by the medical monitor. This is determined on a case-by- case basis.

data.name: Prior and Concomitant Therapy
data.text:
6.9.1.

General Considerations Data on prior treatment with GLP-1 RA or GIP/GLP-1 RA will be collected in CRF per the SoA (Section 1.3). Prior treatment refers to the treatment that was received by the participant before enrollment in the study and discontinued prior to Visit 1.

Participants are permitted to use concomitant medications that they require during the study except medications that may interfere with the assessment of efficacy and safety characteristics of the study interventions.

Participants must consult with the investigator or a designated site staff member if they are prescribed any new medications during the study. If this is not possible due to treatment of medical emergencies, the participant should inform the investigator or a designated site staff member as soon as possible.

The initiation of weight promoting medications is discouraged and alternate therapies not associated with weight gain should be considered whenever possible.

In this study population, many study participants will be taking medications to treat comorbidities, including antihypertensive, diuretic, and lipid-lowering agents, or medications to 65 mitigate GI tolerability, including laxatives and anti-emetics, or medications with weight-based dosing, such as thyroid hormone.

Investigators are responsible for closely monitoring the need to adjust these medications throughout the study. See Section 10.10 for concomitant medication considerations. Discuss medication adjustment as soon as possible with primary care physician or specialist, as applicable.

Recording concomitant medications Site staff will record changes in intensity of medications of special interest on the level of medication intensity CRF at intervals specified in the SoA. These changes should also be recorded in the concomitant medication CRF. Medications of special interest that should be recorded in both CRFs include

• antihypertensive, and

• lipid lowering medications.

Any medication or vaccine, over-the-counter or prescription medicine (including hormonal contraceptives), vitamins or herbal supplements, or other specific categories of interest that the participant is receiving at the time of enrollment or receives during the study must be recorded in the CRF along with

• reason for use

• dates of administration including start and end dates, and

• dosage information including dose and frequency only for concomitant medications of special interest, for example antihypertensive, antihyperglycemic, and lipid lowering medications.

6.9.2.

Prohibited or Restricted Use Medications The following medications are prohibited throughout the study (up to Visit 801):

• antihyperglycemic medications o GLP-1 RA or other incretin-based therapies (for example tirzepatide), pramlintide (amylin analogs), DPP-4 inhibitors (Section 10.9.1.1).

o Use of other antihyperglycemic medications regardless of indication (for example, heart failure and CKD) is prohibited except:

 permanent discontinuation of the study intervention (Section 7.1.1)  rescue therapy due to severe persistent hyperglycemia (Section 6.9.4), or  additional glycemic control during the safety follow-up period.

• subcutaneous/intramuscular or implantable/injectable contraceptives such as Depo- Provera®, Nexplanon®, are prohibited except when initiated and used continuously for at least 18 months prior to study entry, and

• medications intended to promote weight reduction, including prescribed, over the counter, or alternative remedies. Examples are provided in Section 10.9.1.2.

66 Note: Short-term mealtime insulin use for up to 14 days is allowed for certain clinical situations, for example, elective surgery, during hospitalization, and hyperosmolar states, and must be differentiated from mealtime insulin use as rescue therapy when reported in the CRF.

6.9.3.

Prohibited Surgical Treatments or Procedures for Weight Management Surgical treatments, endoscopic therapy, and/or device-based therapy for weight management are not permitted during the study. Refer to Section 5.2 for details.

6.9.4.

Rescue Therapy for Severe Persistent Hyperglycemia Criteria for severe persistent hyperglycemia Investigators will be trained on how to apply decision criteria for the timing and method of intervention in participants who do not reach glycemic targets during the treatment period. An additional therapeutic intervention should be considered in participants who are fully compliant with the assigned therapeutic regimen in the absence of any acute condition that raises BG, AND who meet any of the following criteria:

Criteria for severe persistent hyperglycemia are described in the table below.

If a participant has… An average BG from the once-weekly 4-point SMBG profile of >270 mg/dL (15.0 mmol/L) over at least a consecutive 2-week period any time during the first 8 weeks postrandomization >240 mg/dL (13.3 mmol/L) over at least a consecutive 2-week period at any time 9 to 16 weeks postrandomization >200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) over at least a consecutive 2-week period at any time beyond the first 16 weeks postrandomization HbA1c ≥8.5% (69 mmol/mol) at or after Week 24 with inadequate response to the existing regimen defined as improvement in HbA1c over the last 3 months that is <0.3%.

Abbreviations: BG = blood glucose; HbA1c = hemoglobin A1c; SMBG = self-monitoring of blood glucose.

During the weeks when 7-point SMBG profiles are collected, the once-weekly 4-point SMBG values are included in the 7-point profiles.

6.9.5.

Rescue Medication For participants who meet criteria for severe persistent hyperglycemia, the investigator will decide on an appropriate antihyperglycemic intervention (rescue therapy) that is not a prohibited medication listed in Sections 6.9.2 and 10.9.

If a new antihyperglycemic medication is introduced, metformin should be the first choice of therapy unless contraindicated.

Initiation of insulin as the first rescue intervention for hyperglycemia should be reserved for 67

• participants with severe persistent hyperglycemia with an average BG from the once- weekly 4-point SMBG profile ≥300 mg/dL (≥16.7 mmol/L), or

• participants with symptoms of hyperglycemia, if there is evidence of ongoing catabolism or in other clinical situations where the investigator believes more rapid glycemic control is warranted (ADA 2023).

Participants who receive rescue medicine for hyperglycemia management should also continue administering study intervention for the remaining period in the trial. Record the use of rescue medication as concomitant medication in the CRF.

If any new antihyperglycemic medication is initiated during the safety follow-up period, it will not be classified as rescue therapy.

6.9.6.

Symptomatic Medication for Gastrointestinal Symptoms The investigator may prescribe symptomatic medication for management of GI symptoms as needed during the study, for example, antiemetic or antidiarrheal medication, per local country availability and standard of care (see Section 6.6.1). Record the use of symptomatic medication as concomitant medication in the CRF.

68

data.name: Discontinuation of Study Intervention
data.text:
7.1.1.

Permanent Discontinuation from Study Intervention When necessary, a participant may be permanently discontinued from study intervention. If so, the participant will discontinue the study intervention and will remain in the study and follow procedures for all remaining study visits, as shown in the SoA.

If the participant is unwilling or unable to return for all applicable study visits, the site should attempt to collect as much follow-up information as possible, especially data collection pertaining to primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints at Week 40 of the treatment period.

A participant should be permanently discontinued from study intervention if

• the participant requests to discontinue study intervention

• the participant is diagnosed with acute or chronic pancreatitis, confirmed by adjudication.

See Section 8.3.3.7

• the participant is diagnosed with MTC or MEN2 syndrome

• the participant develops significant elevation of serum calcitonin. See Section 8.3.3.8

• the participant is diagnosed with an active or untreated malignancy (other than basal or squamous cell skin cancer, in situ carcinomas of the cervix, or in situ prostate cancer, for example, Gleason 6 or lower)

• the participant is diagnosed with T1D

• in the opinion of the investigator, for safety reasons

• the participant has intolerable GI symptoms despite management as described in Section 6.6.1

• the participant initiates any other GLP-1 RA or other incretin-based therapies (for example, tirzepatide), pramlintide (amylin analogs), or DPP-4 inhibitors and will not or cannot discontinue the medication

• the participant develops any other TEAE, SAE, or clinically significant laboratory value for which the investigator believes that permanent study intervention discontinuation is the appropriate measure to be taken, or

• the participant becomes pregnant.

Other possible reason which may lead to permanent discontinuation of study intervention include

• if the participant is unable to maintain adequate nutrition or hydration despite management, as described in Section 6.6.2.

• if the participant has a BMI ≤20 kg/m2 (see Section 6.6.3) 69

• the participant has bariatric surgery, body weight reduction procedures, or medications for weight management described in Section 6.9.3

• if the investigator determines that a systemic hypersensitivity reaction has occurred related to study intervention administration, the participant may be permanently discontinued from the study intervention, and the sponsor’s designated medical monitor should be notified. If the investigator is uncertain about whether a systemic hypersensitivity reaction has occurred and whether discontinuation of study intervention is warranted, the investigator may consult the sponsor

• PHQ-9 score ≥15

• C-SSRS o answered “yes” to Question 4 or Question 5 on the “Suicidal Ideation” portion of the C-SSRS, or o answered “yes” to any of the suicide-related behaviors on the “Suicidal Behavior” portion of the C-SSRS.

Note: In the event either the PHQ-9 score or C-SSRS conditions above are met, participants should be referred to a psychiatrist or appropriately trained professional for consultation. If a participant’s psychiatric disorder can be adequately treated with psycho- and/or pharmacotherapy, then the participant, at the discretion of the investigator (in agreement with the psychiatrist or appropriately trained professional), may be continued in the study on study intervention.

Antihyperglycemic therapy after permanent discontinuation of study intervention Following permanent discontinuation of study intervention for any reason, participants may require additional antihyperglycemic therapy to maintain glycemic control. Any locally approved antihyperglycemic therapy that is not a prohibited/restricted medication per Section 10.9 and is not contraindicated for use in the participant may be prescribed in accordance with local prescribing information.

The new antihyperglycemic intervention will be recorded on the concomitant medications CRF.

7.1.2.

Hepatic Criteria for Study Intervention Interruption or Discontinuation See Section 8.2.6.3 for hepatic criteria for study intervention interruption or discontinuation.

7.1.3.

Temporary Interruption of Study Intervention Refer to Sections 6.6 and 8.2.6.3 for information on temporary dose interruptions.

data.name: Participant Discontinuation/Withdrawal from the Study
data.text:
Discontinuation is expected to be uncommon. To minimize the amount of missing data and to enable assessment of study objectives as planned in the study protocol, every attempt will be made to keep participants in the study regardless of study intervention use.

Participants will be discontinued from the study if the participant becomes pregnant.

70 A participant may withdraw from the study

• at any time at the participant’s own request for any reason or without providing any reason

• at the request of the participant’s designee, for example, parents or legal guardian

• at the discretion of the investigator for safety, behavioral, compliance, or administrative reasons, or

• if enrolled in any other clinical study involving an investigational product or enrolled in any other type of medical research judged not to be scientifically or medically compatible with this study.

At the time of discontinuing from the study, if possible, the participant will complete procedures for an ED visit and safety follow-up, as shown in the SoA.

Participants who have discontinued study intervention early and are only willing to come back for Visit 11 (Week 40) are not required to complete a safety follow-up visit if they have been off of study intervention for at least 28 days.

If the participant has not already discontinued the study intervention, the participant will be permanently discontinued from the study intervention at the time of the decision to discontinue the study.

If the participant withdraws consent for disclosure of future information, the sponsor may retain and continue to use any data collected before such a withdrawal of consent.

If a participant withdraws from the study, the participant may request destruction of any samples taken and not tested, and the investigator must document this in the site study records.

data.name: Lost to Follow up
data.text:
A participant will be considered lost to follow-up if they repeatedly fail to return for scheduled visits and are unable to be contacted by the study site. Site personnel or designee are expected to make diligent attempts to contact participants who fail to return for a scheduled visit or were otherwise unable to be followed up by the site.
